'''Balanced number partitioning''' is a variant of [[multiway number partitioning]] in which there are constraints on the number of items allocated to each set. The input to the problem is a set of ''n'' items of different sizes, and two integers&nbsp;''m'',&nbsp;''k''. The output is a partition of the items into ''m'' subsets, such that the number of items in each subset is at most&nbsp;''k''. Subject to this, it is required that the sums of sizes in the ''m'' subsets are as similar as possible.

An example application is [[identical-machines scheduling]] where each machine has a job-queue that can hold at most ''k'' jobs.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal|last1=Zhang|first1=Jilian|last2=Mouratidis|first2=Kyriakos|last3=Pang|first3=HweeHwa|date=2011-06-28|title=Heuristic Algorithms for Balanced Multi-Way Number Partitioning|url=https://www.aaai.org/ocs/index.php/IJCAI/IJCAI11/paper/view/3251|journal=Twenty-Second International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence|language=en}}</ref> The problem has applications also in manufacturing of [[VLSI]] chips, and in assigning tools to machines in [[flexible manufacturing system]]s.<ref name=":52">{{Cite journal|last=Tsai|first=Li-Hui|date=1992-02-01|title=Asymptotic Analysis of an Algorithm for Balanced Parallel Processor Scheduling|url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/0221007|journal=SIAM Journal on Computing|volume=21|issue=1|pages=59–64|doi=10.1137/0221007|issn=0097-5397|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

In the standard [[Optimal job scheduling|three-field notation for optimal job scheduling problems]], the problem of minimizing the largest sum is sometimes denoted by "'''P'''&nbsp;|&nbsp;'''#&nbsp;≤&nbsp;k'''&nbsp;|&nbsp;''C''<sub>max</sub>". The middle field "'''#&nbsp;≤&nbsp;k'''" denotes that the number of jobs in each machine should be at most ''k''. This is in contrast to the unconstrained version, which is denoted by "<math>P\parallel C_\max</math>".<ref name=":9" />

== Two-way balanced partitioning ==
A common special case called '''two-way balanced partitioning''' is when there should be two subsets (''m''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2). The two subsets should contain floor(''n''/2) and ceiling(''n''/2) items. It is a variant of the [[partition problem]]. It is NP-hard to decide whether there exists a partition in which the sums in the two subsets are equal; see <ref name="Garey & Johnson">{{cite book|last1=Garey|first1=Michael|url=https://archive.org/details/computersintract0000gare|title=Computers and Intractability; A Guide to the Theory of NP-Completeness|last2=Johnson|first2=David|year=1979|isbn=978-0-7167-1045-5|pages=[https://archive.org/details/computersintract0000gare/page/96 96–105]|url-access=registration}}</ref> problem [SP12]. There are many algorithms that aim to find a balanced partition in which the sum is as nearly-equal as possible.

* Coffman, Frederickson and Lueker<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Coffman|first1=E. G.|last2=Frederickson|first2=G. N.|last3=Lueker|first3=G. S.|date=1984-05-01|title=A Note on Expected Makespans for Largest-First Sequences of Independent Tasks on Two Processors|url=https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/abs/10.1287/moor.9.2.260|journal=[[Mathematics of Operations Research]]|volume=9|issue=2|pages=260–266|doi=10.1287/moor.9.2.260|issn=0364-765X|url-access=subscription}}</ref>  present a restricted version of the [[LPT algorithm]] (called RLPT), in which inputs are assigned in pairs.  When inputs are uniformly-distributed random variables, the expected largest sum of RLPT is exactly <math>\frac{n}{4}+\frac{1}{2n+2}</math>. The expected work-difference (difference between largest and smallest sum) is <math>\Theta(1/n)</math>.<ref name=":52"/>
* Lueker<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lueker|first=George S|date=1987-12-01|title=A note on the average-case behavior of a simple differencing method for partitioning|url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0167-6377%2887%2990044-7|journal=Operations Research Letters|language=en|volume=6|issue=6|pages=285–287|doi=10.1016/0167-6377(87)90044-7|issn=0167-6377|url-access=subscription}}</ref> presents a variant of the [[Largest differencing method#balanced|LDM algorithm]] (called the pairwise differencing method (PDM)). Its expected work-difference is <math>\Theta(1/n)</math>.
* Tsai<ref name=":52" /> presents an algorithm called Restricted Largest Difference (RLD). Its work-difference is <math>O(\log n/n^2)</math> [[almost surely]].
* Yakir<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Yakir|first=Benjamin|date=1996-02-01|title=The Differencing Algorithm LDM for Partitioning: A Proof of a Conjecture of Karmarkar and Karp|url=https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/abs/10.1287/moor.21.1.85|journal=[[Mathematics of Operations Research]]|volume=21|issue=1|pages=85–99|doi=10.1287/moor.21.1.85|issn=0364-765X|url-access=subscription}}</ref> presents a balanced variant of the [[Largest differencing method|LDM algorithm]] for ''m''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2, called BLDM. Its expected work-difference is <math>n^{-\Theta(\log n)}</math>.
*Mertens<ref>{{cite arXiv|last=Mertens|first=Stephan|date=1999-03-11|title=A complete anytime algorithm for balanced number partitioning|eprint=cs/9903011}}</ref> presents a complete [[anytime algorithm]] for balanced two-way partitioning. It combines the BLDM algorithm with the complete-Karmarkar–Karp algorithm.

== Balanced triplet partitioning ==
Another special case called '''3-partitioning''' is when the number of items in each subset should be at most 3 (''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3). Deciding whether there exists such a partition with equal sums is exactly the [[3-partition problem]], which is known to be [[strongly NP-hard]]. There are approximation algorithms that aim to find a partition in which the sum is as nearly-equal as possible.

* Kellerer and Woeginger<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Kellerer|first1=Hans|last2=Woeginger|first2=Gerhard|date=1993-09-07|title=A tight bound for 3-partitioning|journal=Discrete Applied Mathematics|language=en|volume=45|issue=3|pages=249–259|doi=10.1016/0166-218X(93)90013-E|issn=0166-218X|doi-access=free}}</ref> adapt the [[LPT algorithm]] to triplet partitioning (where there are at most 3*''m'' items, and each subset should contain at most 3 items). Their algorithm is called ''modified-LPT'' or ''MLPT''. It orders the items from large to small, and puts each item in turn into the bin with the smallest sum among those bins that contain fewer than 3 items. They show that the MLPT algorithm attains at most <math>\frac{4 m-1}{3 m}</math> of the ''minimum largest'' sum, which is the same approximation ratio that LPT attains for the unconstrained problem. The bound is tight for MLPT.
* Chen, He and Lin<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Chen|first1=Shi Ping|last2=He|first2=Yong|last3=Lin|first3=Guohui|date=2002-03-01|title=3-Partitioning Problems for Maximizing the Minimum Load|url=https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1013370208101|journal=Journal of Combinatorial Optimization|language=en|volume=6|issue=1|pages=67–80|doi=10.1023/A:1013370208101|s2cid=9053629|issn=1573-2886|url-access=subscription}}</ref> show that, for the same problem, MLPT attains at least <math>\frac{3 m-1}{4 m-2}</math> of the ''maximum smallest'' sum, which is again the same ratio that LPT attains for the unconstrained problem.
* Kellerer and Kotov<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal|last1=Kellerer|first1=Hans|last2=Kotov|first2=Vladimir|date=1999-02-01|title=A 7/6–Approximation Algorithm For 3-Partitioning And Its Application To Multiprocessor Scheduling|url=https://doi.org/10.1080/03155986.1999.11732368|journal=INFOR: Information Systems and Operational Research|volume=37|issue=1|pages=48–56|doi=10.1080/03155986.1999.11732368|issn=0315-5986|url-access=subscription}}</ref> present a different algorithm (for the case with exactly 3*''m'' items), that attains at most <math>7/6</math> of the ''minimum largest'' sum.

== Balanced partitioning with larger cardinalities ==
A more general case, called '''''k''-partitioning''',<ref name=":4" /> is when the number of items in each subset should be at most ''k'', where ''k'' can be any positive integer..
* Babel, Kellerer and Kotov<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Babel|first1=Luitpold|last2=Kellerer|first2=Hans|last3=Kotov|first3=Vladimir|date=1998-02-01|title=The ''k''-partitioning problem|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01193837|journal=Mathematical Methods of Operations Research|language=en|volume=47|issue=1|pages=59–82|doi=10.1007/BF01193837|s2cid=5594197|issn=1432-5217|url-access=subscription}}</ref> study a variant in which there are ''k''×''m'' items (for some integer&nbsp;''k''), and each of the ''m'' sets must contain exactly ''k'' items. They present several heuristic algorithms for approximating the ''minimum largest'' sum:
** ''Folding algorithm'': optimal for ''m''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2, and in general has tight approximation ratio <math>2-\frac{1}{m}</math>.
** ''Exchange algorithm'': tight approximation ratio <math>2-\frac{2}{m+1}</math>. It is not known if it runs in polynomial time.
** ''Primal-dual algorithm'' (a combination of LPT and [[Multifit algorithm|MultiFit]]): approximation ratio at most <math>4/3</math>. It is tight for ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;4 when ''m'' is sufficiently large; the precise lower bound is <math>\frac{4 m}{3 m+1}</math>).<ref name=":4" />{{Rp|Thm.11}}
**The also conjecture that Modified-LPT has an approximation ratio <math>\frac{4 m-1}{3 m}</math> . Currently, this conjecture is known to be true only for ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3.<ref name=":0" /> For ''k''&nbsp;>&nbsp;3, it is known that its approximation ratio is at most 2.<ref name=":9" />
*Michiels, Korst, Aarts, van Leeuwen<ref>{{Citation|last1=Michiels|first1=Wil|title=Performance Ratios for the Differencing Method Applied to the Balanced Number Partitioning Problem|date=2003|url=https://link-springer-com.mgs.ariel.ac.il/chapter/10.1007/3-540-36494-3_51|pages=583–595|place=Berlin, Heidelberg|publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg|doi=10.1007/3-540-36494-3_51|access-date=2021-10-15|last2=Korst|first2=Jan|last3=Aarts|first3=Emile|last4=van Leeuwen|first4=Jan|series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science|volume=2607|isbn=978-3-540-00623-7|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and Spieksma<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal|last1=Michiels|first1=W.|last2=Aarts|first2=E.|last3=Korst|first3=J.|last4=van Leeuwen|first4=J.|last5=Spieksma|first5=F. C. R.|date=2012-02-01|title=Computer-assisted proof of performance ratios for the Differencing Method|journal=Discrete Optimization|language=en|volume=9|issue=1|pages=1–16|doi=10.1016/j.disopt.2011.10.001|issn=1572-5286|doi-access=free}}</ref> study a variant in which each of the ''m'' sets must contain either ceiling(''n''/''m'') or floor(''n''/''m'') items (so ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;ceiling(''n''/''m'')). They extend the Balanced-LDM (BLDM) from ''m''=2 to general ''m''. The generalized algorithm runs in time <math>O(n\log n)</math>.  They prove that its approximation ratio for the minimum largest sum is exactly 4/3 for ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3, 19/12 for ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;4, 103/60 for ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;5, 643/360 for ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;6, and 4603/2520 for ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;7. The ratios were found by solving a [[Mixed integer linear programming|mixed integer linear program]]. In general (for any ''k''), the approximation ratio is at least <math>2-\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\frac{j!}{k!}</math> and at most <math>2-\frac{1}{k-1}</math>. The exact MILP results for 3,4,5,6,7 correspond to the lower bound. For ''k''>7, no exact results are known, but the difference between the lower and upper bound is less than 0.3%.  When the parameter is the number of subsets (''m''), the approximation ratio is exactly <math>2-\frac{1}{m}</math>.
*Zhang, Mouratidis and Pang<ref name=":8" /> show that BLDM might yield partitions with a high work-difference (difference between highest and lowest sum), both when the inputs are distributed uniformly, and when their distribution is skewed. They propose two alternative heuristics: LRM reduces the work-difference to 1/3 the work-difference of BLDM when the distribution is uniform; Meld reduces the work-difference when the distribution is skewed. A [[hybrid algorithm]] combines BLDM, LRM and Meld and adapts dynamically to different data distributions.
*When ''k'' is fixed, a PTAS of Hochbaum and Shmoys<ref name=":02">{{Cite journal|last1=Hochbaum|first1=Dorit S.|last2=Shmoys|first2=David B.|date=1987-01-01|title=Using dual approximation algorithms for scheduling problems theoretical and practical results|journal=Journal of the ACM|volume=34|issue=1|pages=144–162|doi=10.1145/7531.7535|issn=0004-5411|s2cid=9739129|doi-access=free}}</ref> can be used for balanced partitioning.<ref name=":7" /> When ''k'' is part of the input, no PTAS is currently known.<ref name=":7" />
*Dell'Amico and Martello<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal|last1=Dell'Amico|first1=Mauro|last2=Martello|first2=Silvano|date=2001|title=Bounds for the cardinality constrained P∥Cmax problem|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/jos.68|journal=Journal of Scheduling|language=en|volume=4|issue=3|pages=123–138|doi=10.1002/jos.68|issn=1099-1425|url-access=subscription|hdl=11380/15976|hdl-access=free}}</ref> study the problem of minimizing the largest sum when the number of items in all sets is at most ''k''. They show that the linear-program relaxation of this variant has the same optimal value as the LP relaxation of the unconstrained variant. The expression <math>\max((\sum x_i)/m,  x_1)</math>, where ''x<sub>i</sub>'' are the inputs ordered from large to small, is a lower bound for the optimal largest-sum, and its worst-case ratio is 1/2 in both variants. The improved expression <math>\max((\sum x_i)/m, x_1, x_k+x_{m+1})</math> has worst-case ratio 2/3 in the unconstrained variant and 1/2 in the constrained variant. The approximation ratio of the modified [[list scheduling]] is 1/2 for the unconstrained variant, but it is 0 for the constrained variant (it can be arbitrarily bad). The approximation ratio of the modified LPT algorithm is at most 2.  They also show that the lower bound of <ref name=":4" /> has a tight worst-case performance ratio of 3/4, and that their PD algorithm has a tight performance ratio of 4/3 (when ''m'' is sufficiently large).
*He, Tan, Zhu and Yao<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal|last1=He|first1=Yong|last2=Tan|first2=Zhiyi|last3=Zhu|first3=Jing|last4=Yao|first4=Enyu|date=2003-11-01|title=κ-Partitioning problems for maximizing the minimum load|journal=Computers & Mathematics with Applications|language=en|volume=46|issue=10|pages=1671–1681|doi=10.1016/S0898-1221(03)90201-X|issn=0898-1221|doi-access=free}}</ref> consider the problem of maximizing the smallest sum. They show that the FOLDING algorithm has tight approximation ratio <math>\max\left(\frac{2}{k}, \frac{1}{m}\right)</math>. They present a new algorithm, HARMONIC1, with worst-case ratio at least <math>\max\left(\frac{1}{k}, \frac{1}{\lceil \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{1}{i}\rceil+1}\right)</math>. Both these algorithms are ''[[Ordinal data|ordinal]]'' – they partition the items based only on the order between them rather than their exact values. They prove that ''any'' ordinal algorithm has ratio at most <math>O(1/\ln{m})</math>for maximizing the smallest sum. This indicates that HARMONIC1 is [[Asymptotically optimal algorithm|asymptotically optimal]].  For any fixed ''k'', any ordinal algorithm has ratio at most the smallest root of the equation <math>\sum_{i=1}^m \left\lfloor\left\lfloor \frac{k+i-1}{i}\right\rfloor x \right\rfloor = k</math>. When ''k'' tends to infinity, this upper bound approaches&nbsp;0.

=== Relations between balanced and unconstrained problems ===
There are some general relations between approximations to the balanced partition problem and the standard (unconstrained) partition problem.

* Babel, Kellerer and Kotov<ref name=":4" /> prove that the ratio between the unconstrained optimum and the constrained optimum is at most <math>2-\frac{2}{m}</math>, and it is tight.
* Kellerer and Kotov<ref name=":6" /> prove that every heuristic for balanced partitioning with capacity ''k'' and approximation-ratio ''r'' (for the minimum largest sum) can be employed to obtain a heuristic for unconstrained partitioning with approximation-ratio <math>\max\left(r, \frac{k+2}{k+1}-\frac{1}{m(k+1)}\right)</math>. In particular, their <math>7/6</math>-approximation algorithm for triplet partitioning (''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3) can be used to obtain a heuristic for unconstrained partitioning with approximation-ratio <math>\max\left(\frac{7}{6}, \frac{5}{4}-\frac{1}{4 m}\right)</math>.

== Different cardinality constraints ==
The cardinality constraints can be generalized by allowing a different constraint on each subset. This variant is introduced in the "open problems" section of,<ref name=":4" /> who call the '''''k<sub>i</sub>''-partitioning problem'''. He, Tan, Zhu and Yao<ref name=":10" /> present an algorithm called HARMONIC2 for maximizing the smallest sum with different cardinality constraints. They prove that its worst-case ratio is at least <math>\max\left(\frac{1}{k_m}, \frac{k_1}{k_m}\frac{1}{\left\lceil \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{1}{i}\right\rceil+1}\right)</math>.

== Categorized cardinality constraints ==
Another generalization of cardinality constraints is as follows. The input items are partitioned into ''k'' categories. For each category ''h'', there is a capacity constraint ''k<sub>h</sub>''. Each of the ''m'' subsets may contain at most ''k<sub>h</sub>'' items from category ''h''. In other words: all ''m'' subsets should be independent set of a particular [[partition matroid]]. Two special cases of this problem have been studied.

===<span class="anchor" id="kernel"></span>Kernel partitioning===
In the ''kernel balanced-partitioning problem'', some ''m'' pre-specified items are ''kernels'', and each of the ''m'' subsets must contain a single kernel (and an unlimited number of non-kernels). Here, there are two categories: the kernel category with capacity 1, and the non-kernel category with unlimited capacity.
* Chen, He and Yao<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Chen|first1=S. -P.|last2=He|first2=Y.|last3=Yao|first3=E. -Y.|date=1996-09-01|title=Three-partitioning containing kernels: Complexity and heuristic|url=https://link-springer-com.mgs.ariel.ac.il/article/10.1007/BF02247409|journal=Computing|volume=57|issue=3|pages=255–271|doi=10.1007/bf02247409|s2cid=21935917|issn=0010-485X|url-access=subscription}}</ref> prove that the problem is NP-hard even for ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3 (for ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2 it can be solved efficiently by finding a [[maximum weight matching]]). They then present an algorithm called ''Kernel-LPT'' (KLPT): it assigns a kernel to each subset, and then runs the modified [[LPT algorithm]] (puts each item into the subset with the smallest sum among those that have fewer than ''k'' items). They prove that, with ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3, KLPT has an approximation ratio <math>\frac{4 m-1}{3 m}</math> for the ''minimum largest'' sum.<ref name=":3" />{{Rp|3}} However, Chen, He and Lin<ref name=":2" />{{Rp|2}} claim that its tight approximation ratio is <math>\frac{3 m-1}{2 m}</math> for the minimum largest sum,{{Clarify|date=October 2021}} and <math>\frac{2 m-1}{3 m-2}</math> for the maximum smallest sum.

=== One-per-category partitioning ===
In another variant of this problem, there are some ''k'' categories of size ''m'', and each subset should contain exactly one item from each category. That is, ''k''<sub>''h''</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 for each category&nbsp;''h''.

* Wu and Yao<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wu|first1=Biao|last2=Yao|first2=Enyue|date=2007-04-20|title=m-Partitioning problems with partition matroid constraint|journal=Theoretical Computer Science|language=en|volume=374|issue=1|pages=41–48|doi=10.1016/j.tcs.2006.11.016|issn=0304-3975|doi-access=}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wu|first1=Biao|last2=Yao|first2=En-yu|date=2008-03-01|title=Lower bounds and modified LPT algorithm for m-partitioning problems with partition matroid constraint|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s11766-008-0101-8|journal=Applied Mathematics-A Journal of Chinese Universities|language=en|volume=23|issue=1|pages=1–8|doi=10.1007/s11766-008-0101-8|s2cid=16565038|issn=1993-0445|url-access=subscription}}</ref> presented the ''layered LPT'' algorithm – a variant of the [[LPT algorithm]]. They prove that its approximation ratio is <math>2-\frac{1}{m}</math> for minimizing the largest sum; <math>\frac{1}{m}</math> for maximizing the smallest sum in the general case; and in some special cases, can be improved to <math>\frac{m}{2 m-1}</math> for general ''k'' and <math>\frac{m-1}{2 m-3}</math> for ''k''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3. 
* Li and Li<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Li|first1=Weidong|last2=Li|first2=Jianping|date=2013-04-06|title=Approximation algorithms for $$m$$-partitioning problems with partition matroid constraint|url=https://link-springer-com.mgs.ariel.ac.il/article/10.1007/s11590-013-0637-2|journal=Optimization Letters|volume=8|issue=3|pages=1093–1099|doi=10.1007/s11590-013-0637-2|s2cid=3385030|issn=1862-4472|url-access=subscription}}</ref> presented different algorithms for the same problem. For minimizing the largest sum, they present an EPTAS for constant ''k'', and FPTAS for constant ''m''. For maximizing the smallest sum, they present a 1/(''k''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1) approximation algorithm for the general case, and an EPTAS for constant ''k''. They also study a more general objective: minimizing the [[Lp norm|lp-norm]] of the vector of sums. They prove that the layered-LPT algorithm is a 2-approximation algorithm for all norms.
*Dell'Olmo, Hansen, Pallottino and Storchi<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dell’Olmo|first1=Paolo|last2=Hansen|first2=Pierre|last3=Pallottino|first3=Stefano|last4=Storchi|first4=Giovanni|date=2005-09-01|title=On uniform k-partition problems|journal=Discrete Applied Mathematics|language=en|volume=150|issue=1|pages=121–139|doi=10.1016/j.dam.2005.02.013|issn=0166-218X|doi-access=}}</ref> study 32 different objectives for this problem. For each of the four operators max, min, sum, diff, one operator can be applied to the ''k'' items inside each subset, and then one operator can be applied to the ''m'' results for the different subsets. Each of these 16 objectives can be either maximized or minimized, for a total of 32. They show that 21 of these problems can be solved in linear time; 7 require more complex, but still polynomial-time, algorithms; 3 are NP-hard: maximizing (min, sum), minimizing (max, sum) and minimizing (diff, sum). They left open the status of minimizing (diff, diff).

== See also ==
[[Matroid-constrained number partitioning]] is a generalization in which a fixed matroid is given as a parameter, and each of the ''m'' subsets should be an independent set or a base of this matroid.

* Cardinality constraints are special cases of matroid constraints in which the matroid is a [[uniform matroid]]. 
* Categorized cardinality constraints are a special case in which the matroid is a [[partition matroid]].
